subsection: 1. Roles and responsibilities in the family

notes.h: Family life cycle and changing roles
notes.b: Family roles change as members move through stages, and each stage brings different responsibilities.
points: Couple stage: partners set up a shared home and divide household tasks, often according to paid work, time and skills.
Childbearing and child-rearing stage: parents take on the provider, nurturing, educating and socialising roles, and the workload is at its peak.
Adolescent stage: children take on more household tasks and independent responsibilities while parents move from direct control towards guidance.
Launching stage: grown children leave home, and parents' roles change from daily care to advice and support at a distance.
Later life stage: older members may move from giving care to needing it, and adult children often take on practical and financial support for them.
Provider: supplying food, clothing, shelter and money for the family's needs.
Nurturer: giving love, affection and emotional security.
Educator: teaching skills, language, values and good habits through daily routines and example.
Socialiser: introducing children to the norms, beliefs and behaviour expected in family and community.
Protector: ensuring safety, supervising children and making decisions in their best interests.
Manager: planning the household budget, meals, schedules and maintenance of the home.
Disciplinarian: setting boundaries and consequences that are explained and applied consistently.

notes.h: Roles of adolescents in the family
points: Contributing to the household: helping with cooking, cleaning, shopping and minding younger siblings.
Managing their own schoolwork, timekeeping and personal belongings.
Developing independence: making decisions about friends, leisure and part-time work within agreed limits.
Respecting family rules and the privacy of others in shared space.
Some adolescents earn money through part-time work, or give informal care to a sibling or grandparent.
Traditional segregated roles assigned men as breadwinners and women as homemakers and primary carers of children.
Where women work outside the home, they often still carry the larger share of domestic work and childcare.
Men's roles have expanded to include direct childcare, cooking and shared decision-making, and some fathers take the primary caring role.
Gender stereotypes can limit children's roles, for example expecting girls to help in the kitchen and boys to do outdoor jobs.
Sharing household tasks equally reduces overload and resentment, and gives children a model of shared responsibility.
Adult daughters often take on more of the care of ageing parents than sons do.

notes.h: Social and economic factors changing family roles (Higher Level only)
points: Women's participation in paid employment has increased, so many households depend on two earners and domestic roles have had to be shared.
Lone-parent families have increased, so one adult often carries the provider, carer and household roles alone.
Smaller families, by choice or because of later marriage and childbearing, mean each child receives more parental time and money.
Rising housing, childcare and education costs make two incomes necessary for many households, shifting the provider role to both partners.
Longer working hours and commuting reduce the time available for family meals, shared activities and housework.
Longer life expectancy means some families care for parents or grandparents while still raising children, a pattern called the sandwich generation.
Labour-saving appliances reduce the time needed for housework, which allows household tasks to be divided differently.
Greater acceptance of cohabitation, separation and blended families has created new parenting roles, such as step-parent.

notes.b: Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles held by one person cannot be met at the same time.
points: Work-family conflict: a parent is needed at work during the hours a child is ill or has a school event.
Role overload: one person carries too many responsibilities, such as employee, parent, carer and homemaker, for the time available.
Conflict between partners over who does which tasks, or whose career takes priority.
Intergenerational conflict: an adult may have to care for an older parent while still raising children at home.
Consequences include fatigue, reduced quality of parenting, tension between partners and guilt.
Reducing conflict: explicit agreement on the division of tasks, flexible working arrangements, shared decision-making and help from extended family or services.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of stages a family passes through, from couple to childbearing, child-rearing, launching and later life, each with different roles and demands.
The parental responsibility to supply the food, clothing, shelter and money the family needs.
The process through which family members learn language, values, norms and the behaviour expected in their society.
A traditional division of family tasks by gender, with men as breadwinners and women as homemakers and carers.
A household in which both partners are in paid employment.
A family in which one parent has sole day-to-day responsibility for the children.
A clash between the demands of two or more roles held by one person that cannot all be met at the same time.
A situation in which one person has more responsibilities than the time or resources available allow them to fulfil.
Adults who care for ageing parents while also raising or supporting their own children.

factCards.term: Three social factors that have changed family roles
factCards.definition: Increased paid work by women, growth in lone-parent families, and smaller families.

factCards.term: Two economic factors that have changed family roles
factCards.definition: Rising housing and childcare costs that make two incomes necessary, and the longer working hours needed to meet them.

factCards.term: Four responsibilities of adolescents in the family
factCards.definition: Contributing to household tasks, managing their own schoolwork, respecting family rules and privacy, and making responsible decisions within agreed limits.

factCards.term: Two common forms of role conflict
factCards.definition: Work-family conflict, between paid employment and parenting, and role overload, where there are too many roles for the time available.

factCards.term: Three factors that alter a member's role over the life cycle
factCards.definition: Age, health and the number of dependants in the household.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which the roles of family members have changed in recent times.
questions.model: Any three, each with a brief explanation. Women's increased participation in paid employment means that domestic roles and childcare are shared more between partners, or handled by paid services. Smaller families and later childbearing mean parents give each child more time and money. Rising housing and childcare costs mean many households need two incomes, so the provider role is shared by both partners.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the roles and responsibilities of family members change through the family life cycle, and analyse the social and economic factors that have changed these roles.
questions.model: Life cycle: couples share household tasks; during childbearing and child-rearing, parents carry the provider, nurturing, educating, socialising and protecting roles; adolescents take on household tasks and gradual independence while parents move towards guidance; launching brings a shift to advice from a distance; in later life older members may need care and adult children take on practical and financial support. Social factors: more women in paid work, growth of lone-parent and smaller families, later marriage and childbearing, and acceptance of cohabitation and blended families. Economic factors: rising housing, childcare and education costs require two incomes, longer working hours reduce time for household tasks, and labour-saving appliances allow tasks to be divided differently. Full marks need the stages in order, a role or responsibility at each stage, and at least one social and one economic factor explained with its effect on roles.
